1. "With respect to the use of earthern berms, we are inclined to believe that a wall located on the expressway side of Grayland Avenue could be constructed at a lower height than the berms and achieve equivalent acoustical benefits." (p.1)
Whenever a site is shielded from line-of-sight to a source of noise at ground level, the noise levels will be reduced. The degree of attenuation relates to a number of variables including the frequency of the noise, the height and width of the barrier, the proximity of the barrier either to the source of noise or to the listener, and the amount of noise protection the material affords. However, it is absolutely essential that to be an effective shield the barrier must block all residentials level of all buildings from line-of-sight to the road, and it must not have any gaps that would permit noise to leak through.
The sound resistance properties of an earth berm and a solid masonry wall are both fairly high. The dimensions of the barrier becomes an important factor in this instance. The Bolt Beranek and Newman report described on pages 18-22 of the Draft Statement evaluated the effectiveness of a number of shielding barriers of various heights. (A shielding barrier was defined as one that could consist of an earth berm, a continuous wall, or a combination of the two.) The results of their computer calculations demonstrated that the noise protection given by a barrier in the area adjacent to the Expressway varies significantly with the height. The results of the 15 foot barrier are shown on Figure No. 7 in the Statement. The maps on the following pages show the result of the 20 foot and 10 foot barriers. Although a slightly larger area is protected by the 20 foot barier, the differentiation between this height's effect and that of the 15 foot barrier, was judged insignificant in comparison to the disadvantage of the added five feet of shielding: economically more expensive, aesthetically harder to treat, and psychologically more of a wall cutting off the community from the north. On the other hand, the 10-foot high barrier map indicates that the effectiveness of the barrier has been greatly reduced by reducing the height even 5 feet. The 15 foot barrier seems the optimal compromise between limited financial resources, aesthetic and psychological considerations, and the noise impact. The suggestion to lower the height of the barrier would to sacrifice a great deal of noise attenuation to little advantage.
Discussions with the noise consultant on the various types of effective shielding barriers seemed to indicate that where a relatively high barrier is needed adjacent to a residential area, a landscaped berm is a more esthetically pleasing and therefore a more compatible neighboring land use. However, the feasibility of the berm barrier proposed in the Statement will be reassessed
